First let's drop the third party site trying to talk about the Census data and use the Census data directly. Also, the Census also uses, and acknowledges that it uses different, terminology for "small business" than used the Small Business Administration, or politicians. It uses a more colloquial notion of a small business being one that employs less than 500 employees.

So let me break this down into some factoids:

  1. The Census data defines a "small business" as one that employs fewer than 500 people. This is a subset of all legally defined "small businesses" as the SBA (the organization which determines the legal definition of "small business") in many cases allows companies with more than 1,000 employees to be classified as small businesses.

  2. In spite of the fact that the Census data on small business excludes many large companies legally known as "small businesses" it still shows small businesses with fewer than 20 employees as a minority of all small business employers.

  3. The total employment for Census declared "small businesses" is 56,062,893. Small businesses fewer than 20 employees make up 20,408,789 or 36% of this employment. In the "real world" this number is substantially smaller since the SBA legally defines "small business" far more loosely than the Census.

  4. The corollary of #3 is that 64% of small business employment comes "small businesses" with more 20 employees. And again in the "real world" this number is going to be substantially larger since once again the SBA legally defines "small business" far more loosely than the Census.

All of this goes back to what I said, and what you quoted, "...the majority of 'small business' employment is not going to come from mom and pop shops but the companies hundreds to thousands of times their size that still get to call themselves small businesses" which is completely accurate. The point here being that if somebody is working at a small business in the US, they're far more likely to be working at a "small business" than an actual small business. So while you anecdote was interesting, it is not pertinent to the reasons the vast majority of individuals working in "small businesses" are being treated poorly.

From the article, disclosure timeline:

  • April 3, 2015 – Issue reported via the Lastpass ticket system
  • April 4, 2015 – Lastpass responds with confirmation of this issue, confirms they will work on figuring out remediation. (Also discussing a mistake with the link I sent them showing the issue)
  • April 20, 2015 – Patch implemented internally for testing before being pushed to production.
  • April 22, 2015 – Patch pushed to Chrome browser, other browser patches in the works.
  • July 1, 2015 – Mozilla has still not pushed a patch out despite Lastpass submitting it on April 22nd.
